Dealroom · European start-ups with venture funding 2015–2025

What start-ups do, where they are, and who funds them

Question

What does a topic model of start-up descriptions show that the industry labels of a start-up database do not, and how are these topics spread across Europe and linked by cross-border investment?

Short answer

    How we did it

    Step 1: choosing the topic model

    A topic model has settings, and they decide how many topics you get. We tried six combinations. n_neighbors sets how local the map of the descriptions is; min_pts is the smallest group that can become a topic. Each dot is one model.

    Step 2: the topics

    Each dot is a start-up, placed so that start-ups with similar descriptions are close together; the colour is the broad theme of its topic. Hover for the start-up and its topic.

    Step 3: topics and industry labels see different things

    Dealroom gives each start-up one or more of industries. These are markets: health, fintech, energy. A topic model groups start-ups by what their descriptions say. Some topics fall neatly inside one industry; others are spread over many.

    One industry, many topics

    Pick an industry to see which topics its start-ups fall into. The label health covers drug discovery, medical devices, digital mental health and fertility apps, which are different businesses with different investors.

    One topic, many industries

    The other way round: topics whose start-ups are spread over many industries. These are technologies, business models and challenges that cut across markets, and an industry list scatters them.

    Topics without a label

    Dealroom also has finer sub-industries. For these topics, no single sub-industry covers even a quarter of the start-ups: the topic model found a group that the classification has no name for.

    Step 4: where the topics are

    Pick a topic to map it. The colour is the location quotient: how much more common the topic is among a region's start-ups than in Europe as a whole (1 = average, 2 = twice as common). Regions with fewer than 30 funded start-ups are grey.

    Country specialisation

    Pick a theme. Each cell compares the topic's share among a country's start-ups with its share in Europe (RTA; above 1 = specialised). Countries with at least 400 funded start-ups.

    Step 5: who invests where, per topic

    An investment is one investor taking part in one funding round between 2015 and 2025. Its origin is the investor's country compared with the start-up's country.

    Where the money comes from

    The industry average hides the differences

    For each industry, the share of investments from the United States: the industry as a whole (dot) and the range across the topics inside it (bar, topics with at least 100 investments). Hover for the topics at both ends.

    Which country invests in which country

    Rows: country of the investor. Columns: country of the start-up. Pick a topic to see its corridors; the diagonal is domestic investment. The largest 22 investor and 20 start-up countries; the rest are grouped as other.

    What each country invests in abroad

    Pick an investor country: the topics where its cross-border investments are most concentrated, compared with all cross-border investments in Europe (RTA).
